    Neighborhood definition

    Aryan Kamal, Charles Dussiau, Judith Zaugg

    6 March 2026

    neighborhood.Rmd

    Entropy estimation depends on the local neighborhood of each cell.
    For every cell, entropy is computed using the expression values of its neighboring cells.

    The function run_entropy() supports three different ways to define these neighborhoods.

    • auto – neighbors are computed internally using PCA and k-nearest neighbors.
    • seurat – neighbors are supplied as a Seurat Neighbor object.
    • custom – neighbors are supplied manually as a named list.

    This vignette explains how to use each mode.

    Load libraries and example data 

    library(Entropy)
library(Seurat)

data("pbmc_small")
DefaultAssay(pbmc_small) <- "RNA"

    1. Automatic neighborhood computation (auto)

    In "auto" mode, the entropy function computes the neighborhood internally.

    The steps performed internally are:

    1. PCA is computed on a chosen assay.
    2. A k-nearest neighbor graph is built using Seurat::FindNeighbors().
    3. The resulting neighbors are used for entropy estimation.

    By default, neighbors are computed using the same assay used for entropy calculation.
    However, it is often useful to compute neighbors using a different assay.

    For example:

    • entropy may be calculated on raw RNA counts
    • neighborhoods may be computed using SCT-normalized data

    This can be controlled using the parameter:

    neighbor_assay

    If not specified, neighbor_assay defaults to the same assay used for entropy.

    Example: neighbors automatically computed from the RNA assay.

    res_auto <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors = NULL,
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  mode = "counts"
)

    Example: compute entropy on RNA but build neighborhoods from the SCT assay.

    # example only (pbmc_small does not contain an SCT assay)
# res_auto_sct <- run_entropy(
#   seu = pbmc_small,
#   assay = "RNA",
#   neighbor_assay = "SCT",
#   neighbors_method = "auto",
#   add_assay = FALSE,
#   mode = "counts"
# )

    Key parameters used in this mode:

    • neighbors = NULL → tells the function to compute neighbors automatically
    • neighbors_method = "auto" → activates internal neighbor computation
    • neighbor_assay → assay used to compute the neighbor graph
    • k → number of nearest neighbors
    • npca → number of PCA dimensions used for neighbor search

    2. Using a Seurat Neighbor object (seurat)

    In some workflows, neighbors may already be computed outside the entropy function.
    For example, a user may want to reuse a neighbor graph already created during clustering.

    In this case, a Seurat Neighbor object can be passed directly.

    First we compute neighbors using Seurat.

    pbmc_small <- RunPCA(pbmc_small)

pbmc_small <- FindNeighbors(
  pbmc_small,
  reduction = "pca",
  dims = 1:10,
  return.neighbor = TRUE,
  graph.name = "example_nn"
)

nn_obj <- pbmc_small@neighbors[["example_nn"]]

    The object nn_obj is a Seurat Neighbor object that contains the indices of neighboring cells.

    We can now pass this object directly to run_entropy().

    res_seurat <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors = nn_obj,
  neighbors_method = "seurat",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  mode = "counts"
)
    ## INFO [2026-03-06 14:37:21] Assay 'RNA' found and set as default assay.
## INFO [2026-03-06 14:37:21] Starting entropy estimation for assay: RNA
## INFO [2026-03-06 14:37:21] Assay 'RNA' contains 80 cells and 230 features
## INFO [2026-03-06 14:37:21] Using user-provided Seurat neighbor object.
## INFO [2026-03-06 14:37:21] Reading the precomputed table (counts mode)
    head(res_seurat)
    ##                    means
## ATGCCAGAACGACT 0.5741786
## CATGGCCTGTGCAT 0.6153411
## GAACCTGATGAACC 0.7568002
## TGACTGGATTCTCA 0.5944679
## AGTCAGACTGCACA 0.5741786
## TCTGATACACGTGT 0.5741786

    Key parameters in this mode:

    • neighbors = nn_obj → the Seurat Neighbor object
    • neighbors_method = "seurat" → tells the function how to interpret the object

    This mode is useful when:

    • neighbors are already computed
    • a specific neighbor graph should be reused
    • entropy should match an existing analysis pipeline

    3. Custom neighborhood list (custom)

    In "custom" mode, neighbors are supplied manually.

    The neighbors must be provided as a named list where:

    • each element corresponds to one cell
    • the name of the element is the cell name
    • the value is a vector of neighbor cell names or indices

    Example structure:

    neighbors[["cell_A"]] = c("cell_B", "cell_C", "cell_D")
neighbors[["cell_B"]] = c("cell_A", "cell_D", "cell_E")

    Each cell must appear in the list.

    Creating a custom neighbor list

    To illustrate the structure, we convert the Seurat neighbor object into a custom list.

    cell_names <- colnames(pbmc_small)

custom_neighbors <- setNames(
  lapply(seq_along(cell_names), function(i) {
    neighbor_idx <- nn_obj@nn.idx[i, ]
    cell_names[neighbor_idx]
  }),
  cell_names
)

    Run entropy using custom neighbors 

    res_custom <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors = custom_neighbors,
  neighbors_method = "custom",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  mode = "counts"
)

    Key parameters:

    • neighbors = custom_neighbors → the neighbor list
    • neighbors_method = "custom" → tells the function to interpret the list

    Summary

    The entropy function supports three flexible ways to define neighborhoods:

    Mode Input Typical use
    auto none simplest option, neighbors computed internally
    seurat Seurat Neighbor object reuse neighbors from Seurat workflows
    custom named list fully user-defined neighborhood structure

    For most users, "auto" mode is recommended.
    Advanced users can supply Seurat or custom neighbors to integrate entropy estimation into existing pipelines.
